analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal eviction moratorium to all renters and bans late fees during the pandemic.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a committee referral; no Senate vote was ever held before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the CARES Act eviction moratorium so it protected every renter in the country, not just those living in federally backed housing. It would have extended the moratorium to March 27, 2021, barred landlords from charging late fees or penalties tied to unpaid rent, and required a 30-day notice before a renter could be told to leave for nonpayment after the moratorium ended. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters — including the roughly 43 million renter households named in the bill's findings, and especially the millions who spend most of their income on housing — who could not pay rent after pandemic job losses. The bill would have stopped eviction filings for nonpayment nationwide and prevented fee stacking that adds debt on top of unpaid rent.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the CARES Act eviction moratorium to all tenants, not just tenants of federally assisted properties, closing a gap that left most renters unprotected.
Extends the moratorium until March 27, 2021; the existing moratorium was set to expire July 25, 2020, weeks after the bill was introduced.
Prohibits landlords from charging fees, penalties, or other charges related to nonpayment of rent during the moratorium.
Requires a 30-day notice period before a tenant can be required to vacate for nonpayment after the moratorium expires.

The bill cites data that more than 40 million people had filed for unemployment claims since the pandemic began, and that 20.8 million renters spent more than 30 percent of income on housing, as the basis for the public-health rationale of keeping people housed.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords, who would be unable to file evictions for nonpayment or collect late fees during the moratorium. The bill did not include rental assistance to offset landlords' lost rent, so property owners — including small landlords with mortgages of their own — would carry unpaid rent balances until the moratorium expired.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed the moratorium without any rental assistance or relief for landlords, who would still owe mortgages, taxes, and maintenance while barred from collecting rent or fees; small landlords could face their own financial distress.

Unpaid rent would accumulate as debt during the moratorium, and tenants would still owe the full balance once the 30-day post-moratorium notice period ran out, setting up a wave of eviction cases afterward.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered strong protection to renters facing pandemic job losses at a real but arguably diffusable cost to landlords — costs some landlords would have borne indefinitely without any compensation attached. An honest supporter would acknowledge that a moratorium alone shifts cash-flow problems rather than solving them, and that pairing it with rental assistance would have been fairer to small property owners. As a temporary pandemic health measure, its benefits to renters and public health were substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 29, 2020 with 16 Democratic and one Independent cosponsors, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Banking Committee ranking member Sherrod Brown.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced.
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and the rental industry: the expanded nationwide moratorium on evictions and late fees was never enacted, and the broader CARES Act moratorium expired as scheduled in late July 2020 without this extension.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Banking Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have barred eviction filings and late-fee collection nationwide for nearly nine months, and extended a 30-day notice requirement afterward. It would have shifted unpaid-rent costs onto property owners without compensation.

industries.industry: Eviction filing and debt-collection services (process servers, collection firms)
industries.note: A nationwide moratorium on eviction filings for nonpayment would have eliminated the case volume these businesses rely on during the period it covered.

industries.industry: Multifamily housing investors and property management firms
industries.note: They would have absorbed deferred rent like other landlords, but the bill was temporary and left lease terms, and rent owed, intact after expiration.
